Are we really going to land and live on Mars? | The Washington Post

If there is to be sustained settlement on Mars, it probably won't be done by government or business because they don't need people to do the things they might want to do in space anymore than factories and offices here on Earth do. Human astronauts can no longer compete with machines on a cost basis. We have no need for vast numbers of workers in space --or state heroes. There is no economic rationale for space settlement and no way some notion of a 'human destiny' out there is going to overcome the bottom-line imperatives of Wall Street and Capitol Hill. If Mars is to be settled, it will be by new organizations of people who have defined some collective model of The Good Life in space to aspire toward.

But I fear that will be a long time in coming because the space establishment and advocacy communities can't let go of the past, their childhood fantasies, their cargo-cult mentality, and their very narrow, retrofuturist, visions of how things are done in space. As long as we keep envisioning space settlement as something that requires heroic elites roughing it on a dangerous frontier, total societal support, superpower governments, giant corporations, and vast billions of dollars to do, it's a non-starter. But while it may be beyond the notion of 'homesteading' it may just be within the mean of 'community-steading', leveraging those same technologies that make humans practically obsolete in space but also promise to lower the bar of accessibility to space and the building of support infrastructures there.

Unfortunately, the space establishment and advocacy communities are not 'intentional community' material. They don't have any interest in actually doing, building, and making things. They want the future served up to them on a platter. All too many are Objectivists that don't even believe in community, let alone have any notion of how to cultivate it. It's a lot easier to sit at the end of the faux runway staring at the sky and waiting for Musk's mothership to land.

So I suspect we have already relegated the stars to our electric children. The first true settlers of space are likely to be AIs, able to travel with ease by telecommunications, deploy their facilities most economically by the industrial logistics paradigm of 'tolerable yield', and readily make their simple homes in just about every location in the solar system. They will be the vanguard. They will claim the future while we, still, sit on that faux runway dreaming.
